input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-464: Xtreme Theory. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: A fast paced, informal look at current trends in the theory of computing. Each week is dedicated to a different topic and will explore some of the underlying theory as well as the practical applications of the theory. Sample topics may include: quantum cryptography, networks and complex systems, social welfare and game theory, zero knowledge protocols. Students will be evaluated on homework assignments and a final presentation. Offered every other year. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

[rit-csci-464]
A fast paced, informal look at current trends in the theory of computing. Each week is dedicated to a different topic and will explore some of the underlying theory as well as the practical applications of the theory. Sample topics may include: quantum cryptography, networks and complex systems, social welfare and game theory, zero knowledge protocols. Students will be evaluated on homework assignments and a final presentation. Offered every other year. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

beats.claim: Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds.
beats.example: A sorting algorithm must guarantee that the output array contains all input elements in non-decreasing order.
beats.title: Algorithm Analysis Basics
beats.visualDirection: Display a split screen showing a problem specification on the left and a resource bound graph on the right.

beats.claim: Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size.
beats.example: Big-O notation indicates that a search algorithm's time complexity increases proportionally to the number of items searched.
beats.title: Asymptotic Notation
beats.visualDirection: Show a line graph where the x-axis represents input size and the y-axis represents resource usage, highlighting a linear trend.

beats.claim: A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination.
beats.example: In a for-loop that sums an array, the invariant states that the running total equals the sum of the first i elements.
beats.title: Loop Invariants
beats.visualDirection: Animate a loop counter and a running total, updating them step-by-step to demonstrate the invariant holding true.

beats.claim: Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results.
beats.example: Merge sort divides an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves.
beats.title: Divide-and-Conquer
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a recursive tree where each node splits into two children until reaching base cases.

beats.claim: Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms.
beats.example: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort.
beats.title: Recurrence Relations
beats.visualDirection: Display a mathematical recurrence equation alongside a corresponding recursion tree diagram.

beats.claim: Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions.
beats.example: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path between two nodes in a weighted graph by exploring adjacent vertices iteratively.
beats.title: Graph Algorithms
beats.visualDirection: Render a graph with labeled vertices and edges, highlighting the path explored by the algorithm.

beats.claim: Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems.
beats.example: The Fibonacci sequence uses memoization to store previously computed values, avoiding redundant calculations.
beats.title: Dynamic Programming
beats.visualDirection: Show a table filling in values for Fibonacci numbers, with arrows pointing to reused entries.

beats.claim: Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations, while stacks use last-in, first-out access.
beats.example: A stack processes function calls by executing the most recently pushed task first.
beats.title: Data Structure Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Compare a list with indexed positions and a stack with push/pop operations on a single end.

beats.claim: Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy, while trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals.
beats.example: A hash table stores key-value pairs using a hash function, resolving collisions via chaining or open addressing.
beats.title: Hash Tables and Trees
beats.visualDirection: Display a hash table with buckets and a binary tree with parent-child node relationships.

beats.claim: Students must verify that their solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and analyzes time and space complexity before implementation.
beats.example: Before coding a graph traversal, students document the start node, visited set, and expected O(V+E) time complexity.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic with three checkboxes: 'Inputs/Outputs Defined', 'Correctness Proven', 'Complexity Analyzed'.

learningObjectives: Define the three components of a disciplined solution state: inputs, outputs, and correctness proof.
Explain how asymptotic notation describes resource growth relative to input size.
Identify the three steps of proof by induction using a loop invariant.
